Subject: Patchwork CI now works on GitLab

Hi,

From November 12, Patchwork CI quarantines flaky tests on GitLab CI as well as GitHub Actions. Same as before: when a test fails and then passes on retry, we flag it and stop it from blocking the pipeline.

It's free for open-source projects on GitLab too.

Connect a GitLab project here: patchworkci.dev/gitlab

Tomas Berg

Our first big customer left Ledgerline after 5 months.

They had customised NetSuite heavily, and we only handled the standard fields. For a setup like theirs, we simply didn't fit.

We spent the next 6 weeks adding support for custom fields.

We have 38 customers now. 11 of them use custom fields.

What I took from it: when a customer leaves, ask which part of their real setup you didn't handle. It's usually something specific, and you can usually build it.

When we started Fernway Studio, we billed by the hour. 4 of our first 6 projects went over budget, and clients were as frustrated as we were.

In 2024 we switched to a fixed price: KES 450,000 for a Shopify store.

The client knows the number before we start. If we run slow, that's our problem, not theirs.

We've launched 31 stores since. 2 ran past our 6-week timeline.

If you run a services business and keep going over budget, try writing down the fixed number you'd charge. If you can't, you probably don't understand the job well enough yet.

Patchwork CI is on 1,200 repositories now. About 900 of them are open source, where it's free.

The free tier gave us something I didn't expect: data. Across all those repos, 1 in 7 CI failures turned out to be a flaky test, not a real bug.

The open-source maintainers also told us what to build next. GitLab support was their most-requested feature. We shipped it on November 12.

If you're deciding whether a free tier is worth it for a dev tool: for us, it paid off in data and direction before it paid in money.

Pebble Pantry now has 1,000 families paying €4.99 a month.

I started building it 14 months ago, on maternity leave, mostly because I kept standing in front of the fridge at 7pm with no plan.

We didn't get here through ads. Most families found us in school WhatsApp groups, one parent telling another. I can't take credit for that.

So thank you to whoever first dropped the link in their class group. If you're building a consumer app for parents, find out which group chats they're in. That's where the recommendations happen.

The first Rotaship was a standalone mobile app. In its first month, 12% of restaurant staff opened it.

The problem wasn't the app. Restaurant staff already live in WhatsApp, and we were asking them to open something else.

In 2025 we moved the schedules into WhatsApp. Staff get their shifts there and swap them there.

We're in 140 outlets now. The median time for staff to reply to a shift message is 20 minutes.

If your users already have a habit, build inside it. It's less fun to design for, but people actually use it.

Quietroom is hiring its first account executive.

Every one of the 210 booths we've sold so far was sold by me. That got us here. It won't get us to the next 210.

The job: London, 3 days a week in the office. £55,000 base plus commission.

You'd be taking over sales I've been running on my own, so you'd be building how we sell, not following a playbook.

The link to apply is in the comments.

Mark Hollis

I worked in a vet clinic for 11 years. The part I never got used to was sedating anxious animals just so we could examine them.

In 2023 I started Doorstep Vet so I could see those animals at home instead, where they feel safest.

There are 4 of us now, doing about 30 home visits a week.

Dr. Amelia Chen

In September we raised Tabwise from $8 to $12 per user per month.

The reason: our support cost per customer had doubled since launch, and the price hadn't moved.

Everyone who was already paying kept $8 for 12 months.

In the 2 months after, 2 of our 140 customers left.

I expected it to be worse. If your costs have moved and your price hasn't, look at the real numbers before you decide you can't raise it.

Our first production run at Shelfwise had a fault. 400 labels went out with a bad battery contact.

We recalled all 400 and replaced them at our cost. That came to about $7,000.

Then we added a contact test at the factory for every label, not a sample.

We've shipped 6,000 labels since. None have failed on the contact.

The lesson for other hardware founders is the boring one: test every unit for whatever failed, at the factory, before it ships.

2,000 freelancers used Kopa during the private beta. Between them, they invoiced KES 84 million, and their clients paid by M-Pesa.

The request we heard most was for invoices in US dollars. It's on the roadmap.

The public beta opens on March 4, for any freelancer in Kenya.

Thank you to the 2,000 who used it early and told us what to fix.

I was a maintenance engineer at an auto-parts plant in Pune when a spindle failed and stopped a line for 3 days.

The vibration readings had shown the problem 2 weeks earlier. Nobody was watching them.

That's why I started Ferrous in 2022: so someone is watching.

Our sensors are on 410 machines across 17 plants now.

If you run a plant, ask who would notice if a vibration reading changed this week. If the answer is "nobody in particular," that's the gap.

Crateful passed $50,000 in monthly recurring revenue. It took 18 months, with no outside funding and a team of 3.

The most useful thing I can share is where the customers came from. About 60% of signups came through our Shopify App Store listing.

If you're building on a platform with an app store, look at how your listing reads to a stranger before you spend money anywhere else.

Linguo Labs is 14 people in Estonia, Latvia, Finland and Sweden. A few things that work for us:

Most of the work is written down and reviewed asynchronously, so people can do focused work on their own schedule.

Wednesdays have no meetings.

Twice a year, the whole team meets in person in Tallinn.

None of this is new. It works because we stick to it.

Our 100th rooftop went up this week, on a mechanic's workshop in Mooca.

The first one was 2 years ago. Every one of the 100 was a lease with R$ 0 upfront.

We promise installation in 21 days. Across the 100, the average was 19.

Thank you to our team, and to the first owners who signed with us when we had nothing to show them.

I shot weddings for 9 years, about 40 a season. A wedding gave me around 3,000 photos, and culling them took most of a working day.

That was the part of the job I'd have paid someone else to do. Nobody could, because the decisions were mine.

Halftone does the boring part of those decisions: it flags blinks, blur and near-duplicates. In testing it got through 3,000 photos in 6 minutes. You still choose the keepers.

It runs inside Lightroom Classic and costs $15 a month.

Until January, Northbound Talent charged 25% of first-year salary, like most agencies. Our average fee came to about $41,000 per hire.

The problem with a percentage is that the recruiter earns more when you pay more. I didn't like having that sitting behind every salary conversation.

Since January we charge a flat $18,000 per hire. We only place senior Rust engineers, which makes a flat fee easier to set.

We've placed 26 this year. I can't tell you yet whether a flat fee works for generalist recruiting. For a narrow niche like ours, it has.

Title: Show HN: Patchwork CI, quarantine flaky tests in GitHub Actions

Hi HN, we're Tomas and Ines. Patchwork CI is a GitHub app for flaky tests. When a test fails in GitHub Actions, it reruns it. If it passes on retry, we mark it flaky and quarantine it, so it stops blocking merges. Free for open source, $10 per private repo per month. We'd like to hear where the detection gets it wrong. patchworkci.dev
